analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on carbon pollution and returns most of the money to workers and retirees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: the Senate Finance Committee took no action after it was referred in April 2019, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge fees on coal, oil, natural gas, and fluorinated greenhouse gases, starting at $52 per ton of carbon dioxide and rising each year until U.S. emissions fall to 20% of 2005 levels. It would return the money to workers through a tax credit of up to $900 ($1,800 for couples), pay the same amount annually to Social Security, disability, and veterans' beneficiaries, and send $10 billion a year to states to help low-income and rural households and to retrain fossil fuel workers. The fees would make gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity more expensive, but the credits and payments would more than cover those costs for most lower-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and retirees: a refundable tax credit of up to $900 for workers ($1,800 for joint filers), an annual payment of the same size to Social Security, disability, railroad retirement, and veterans' beneficiaries, state grants for household rebates to low-income people (household income up to 150% of the poverty line), and job training prioritized for fossil fuel workers [S3]. Cleaner-energy industries would gain as the fee shifts costs away from fossil fuels [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Workers receive a refundable credit equal to the lesser of 6.2% of earned income or $900 ($1,800 on joint returns), and the credit is ignored when deciding eligibility for other federal benefit programs [S3].
Social Security, disability, railroad retirement, and veterans' beneficiaries receive an annual payment equal to the same $900 amount, disbursed each spring [S3].

Each state gets a share of a $10 billion annual grant program, which must partly fund monthly rebates to low-income individuals and can fund rural energy-cost assistance and job training with priority for fossil fuel workers [S3].
The fee starts at $52 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2020 and rises 6% plus inflation each year, and it only stops growing once U.S. emissions fall below 20% of 2005 levels [S3].
Fees also cover methane and other leaks from the coal, oil, and gas supply chains after 2022, so companies cannot dodge the fee by venting or flaring gas [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers pay the fees, and costs would flow into gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households whose credits or payments do not fully cover their higher energy costs — for example people with little or no earned income who are not on Social Security or disability — would bear some of the difference. Exporters are refunded and imports face an equal fee, which is meant to shield U.S. manufacturers from competitors abroad [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise prices on gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity for every household, and the offset credit is capped at $900 per worker ($1,800 per couple), so people outside the covered groups — such as working-age adults with no earnings who are not on disability — would absorb some of the increase [S3].

A carbon fee this high and rising is a large new tax stream through the Treasury; critics of carbon pricing argue it raises energy costs across the economy, and the bill's own design shows its authors judged the price increases large enough to require a federal rebate system, border fees on imports, and $10 billion a year in state aid to hold households harmless [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Most of the revenue is returned directly to working and retired households, and the bill is structured so lower-income people come out ahead after accounting for higher energy prices. The main weakness is at the edges: workers with no earnings who are not beneficiaries, and households whose energy costs are unusually high relative to the capped credit, would not be fully compensated. The $52 starting fee and automatic yearly increases are aggressive, but that is the point of the design — and the bill would rise until emissions fall to a fifth of 2005 levels.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2019, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 10, 2019 with three original cosponsors: Senators Schatz, Heinrich, and Gillibrand [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the same day; the committee took no further action, and no other action ever appears in the bill's history [S5].
The bill finished with three cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers avoided the fees, and energy-intensive manufacturers avoided the border charges; no consumer received the credits or rebates. Chair Chuck Grassley's Finance Committee was better off with the option never exercised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; workers never got the rebates

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on April 10, 2019; the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, and it died without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four Senate supporters were Democrats (Whitehouse plus three cosponsors), no Republican cosponsored it, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges these companies $52 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2020, rising each year, plus a supplementary fee covering methane leaks from their supply chains after 2022 [S3]. Their revenue depends on the fuels the bill prices away from.

They would pay carbon fees on their energy inputs, but the bill refunds fees on exported goods and charges an equalizing fee on comparable imports, so U.S. factories are not undercut by producers in countries with no carbon fee [S3].
Companies that capture and securely store carbon dioxide emitted from burning fossil fuels get the fee refunded, creating a direct financial reward for capture, storage, and utilization [S3].
Production and import of HFCs, SF6, and similar gases face a phased-in fee reaching its full amount in 2031, with refunds only for goods that destroy or permanently transform the gases [S3].
A steadily rising fee on fossil fuels makes wind, solar, nuclear, and efficiency relatively cheaper, shifting energy investment away from coal, oil, and gas [S3].
